title: Webhook notification event
description: One revision of one alert about one train for one subscription. Delivery is at-least-once with no ordering guarantee, so a receiver MUST apply three suppression rules before it dispatches anything natively: drop a duplicate event_id; drop a revision not strictly newer than the highest applied for that alert_id; and never dispatch a `predicted` revision for a train already `confirmed`, whatever its revision. Duplicate suppression and revision ordering within our stream are supplied as a client policy, not left as homework.

schema_version.description: Refuse a shape your receiver does not know rather than mis-parse it. Every client step on our side fails closed the same way.

event_id.description: Immutable, and deterministic over (alert_id, revision) so a re-run of the same decision mints the same id and your inbox recognises the duplicate. It is NOT a capability: it must never become a lookup key or a bearer credential.

type.description: A new revision is minted only on a lifecycle transition -- first warning, predicted to confirmed, or withdrawal. A changed probability, delay figure or wording mints NOTHING, at any size: there is no materiality threshold, because minting on any changed figure would turn every ingestion cycle into a fresh revision and a second notification about the same train.

phase.description: `predicted` is a forecast from our models. `confirmed` is a cancellation the operator's own real-time feed has already declared, of the boarding call or (since 2026-10-19) of the destination call while the vehicle still leaves -- either way the traveller cannot make the trip on this departure, and `payload.arrival.cancelled` says which end failed. A fact, not a forecast, which is why its probabilities are 1.0 and its delay figures are null (every one of them meant "if it runs"). `withdrawn` means the FORECAST changed, not that normal service is guaranteed.

alert_id.description: The canonical per-train subject key, and the only key the supplied policy deduplicates and orders on. The grain is (subscription, train): a client serves many commuters through one receiver, and a per-train-only key would make the receiver's own revision rule suppress the SECOND commuter's notification about the same disrupted train. The train's own fields below ride along for display and for your joins; they are not the identity.

revision.description: Strictly increasing per alert_id. Monotonicity is structural rather than a property of our clock: it is seeded from a UTC instant and then clamped to max(stored + 1, seed) inside the transaction, so it survives an autumn DST fall-back and an NTP step backwards. A revision formatted from a local timestamp would go backwards for an hour every October and a receiver ordering on it would silently discard every event for those subjects, a confirmed cancellation included.

occurred_at.description: When we decided this revision, UTC.

valid_until.description: How long this event is worth acting on: the earlier of a 60-minute horizon from occurred_at and the train's EXPECTED departure -- its aimed time plus the delay we predict for it, which is also what decides whether the train can still be caught, so a train running 25 minutes late stays valid past its aimed time. An expected departure less than two minutes ahead of occurred_at when the event is minted -- already past included -- is floored to two minutes ahead, so an observation made moments before the train leaves is still attempted once; valid_until is never earlier than occurred_at plus two minutes. WHERE EACH TERM IS ENFORCED, stated rather than implied -- those two are applied to the value you receive, while the subscription's own lifetime is enforced at dispatch instead: we re-read the live subscription immediately before every attempt and stop sending once it has ended. So for a subscription that expires inside this horizon you may hold an event whose valid_until outlives it by up to an hour. Nothing further is sent for it, and the value bounds YOUR dispatch window rather than asserting the subscription still exists. Past valid_until the event is expired rather than failed. The retry INTERVAL is deliberately not published as a constant: it is one attempt per notification pass, and the pass runs on SIRI ingestion changes -- measured at a ~296 s period on 2026-09-08, which is a measurement rather than a schedule.

subscription_version.description: The subscription version this event was authorised by. Deletion or expiry stops later claims, and we recheck eligibility immediately before dispatch -- but a request already in flight may complete, so your receiver rechecks the recipient mapping too.

external_ref.description: Your own opaque reference from the subscription, echoed unchanged.

test.description: True for a synthetic test event. It rides INSIDE the signed body, so a receiver can refuse it before native dispatch; it is not a header a proxy can strip. Only subscriptions marked test-only at creation can produce one, and that marker is immutable.

operator.description: Codespace of the operator, e.g. VYG.

journey_ref.description: The dated service journey reference. A Vy train missing from today's timetable (only ever on the public journey-alerts read, never in an event) carries the synthetic `RemovedJourney:<train number>_<yyyy-mm-dd>` instead, which resolves nowhere else.

stop_place.description: The boarding stop place this alert is about -- the subscription's origin, or the ref of the same physical place the feed recorded the call on.

situations.description: The contributing SIRI-SX situation numbers. Several situations about one disruption are collapsed to ONE event per train, so this can name more than one. A synthetic `KIX:`-prefixed number means there is no operator message behind the alert: either the real-time feed declared the cancellation with no situation published, or the alert rests on real-time data alone. `KIX:PlanRemoved:` (a Vy train missing from today's timetable) never appears: no event is minted for one, and the public journey-alerts read lists it instead.

payload.description: The facts plus the Norwegian prose. Normal receipt needs no second request to us.

title.description: The fact about the train, e.g. «Tog L1 07:18 er innstilt». Norwegian, and identical to what /varsel would have pushed for the same journey.

body.description: The route on its own first line, then the wording. Norwegian. Never varies by branding: the wording is what our own feedback loop records, and text that varied per variant would split every wording comparison along a second axis.

action.description: An optional deep link or label the client may render.

call.description: The affected call, as both producers actually emit it: `stop_place`, `stop_order`, `aimed_departure_time` and `departs_tomorrow`. AIMED, never expected -- the real-time estimate for this call is what the probabilities and the delay figures beside it are derived from, and restating it here as a second time would invite a receiver to display a figure the forecast has already superseded. Boarding and alighting permissions are not carried either: they gate the MATCH upstream (calling at a stop is not the same as being usable from it -- long-distance runs are routinely sold boarding-only over their local stretch), so a call you receive is one the traveller may board and alight at, and repeating the flags would publish a rule instead of its result.

probabilities.description: Impact and cancellation probabilities at the BOARDING call; `arrival` carries the destination call's. Both are 1.0 and the delay figures are null when `phase` is `confirmed`, including a confirmed cancellation of the destination call: the trip is then as impossible as if the boarding call were cancelled.

delay.description: Delay figures, or null for a confirmed cancellation.

arrival.description: The same vehicle journey at the subscription's destination stop: `stop_place`, `stop_order`, `aimed_arrival_time`, `cancelled` (the real-time feed has declared that call cancelled), `cancellation` (P(cancelled) there, 0-1), `delay_ge10` (P(arrival >= 10 min late | it runs)) and `delay` (`{typical_min, worst_case_min}` arrival delay, or null). `probabilities` and `delay` beside it describe the BOARDING call. A vehicle can leave and still never reach the destination: when the feed has declared the destination call cancelled, the event is `phase` `confirmed` with `effect` `cancelled` and `probabilities` at 1.0 like a boarding cancellation (since 2026-10-19), and `arrival.cancelled` true beside a running `call` is how to tell the two apart. A forecast here (`cancellation`) moves nothing. Like `delay_ge10` and `delay`, every figure that means 'if it runs' is null when `cancelled` is true. Null when we could not resolve the destination call, and absent from an event minted before the field existed.

destination.description: Where the train terminates, as a departure board names it (`Drammen`), and the same value `notification.title` names the train with: «Tog R14 Drammen 14:59». Null when we do not know it, which today is every train but Vy's and every bus. Absent from an event minted before the field existed.

mode.description: The line's transport mode in the Journey Planner's own `TransportMode` vocabulary: `rail`, `bus`, `metro`, `tram`, `water`, `coach`, ... It is the LINE's mode, so a replacement bus on a rail line is `rail`. Never null for a rail line. For any other line it is null only when the Journey Planner could not be reached as we started, until it answers, normally within a minute. Absent from an event minted before the field existed.

situations.description: The contributing situations, each with `situation_number`, the Norwegian `summary` and `description`, their English `summary_en` and `description_en`, `en_machine_translated`, their nynorsk `summary_nn` and `description_nn`, `nn_machine_translated`, `has_situation` and `report_type`. `report_type` is SIRI-SX's `reportType` as the operator published it, `INCIDENT` or `GENERAL`, and null for a `KIX:` situation (no operator message) or one that carried none; absent from an event minted before the field existed. The English is the operator's own where they published one (Vy does on every situation), the service's own for a `KIX:` situation (whose Norwegian it also wrote), and otherwise a machine translation of the Norwegian, with `en_machine_translated` true -- present that as a translation, not as the operator's words. The nynorsk is the service's own for a `KIX:` situation and otherwise ALWAYS a machine translation, with `nn_machine_translated` true, because no operator publishes nynorsk. A translation can land a poller cycle after the situation first appears, and until one does that language's three fields are null; the nynorsk fields are absent from an event minted before they existed.

situations_text.description: The `situations` as ONE Norwegian text, for showing in place of every `description` stacked: the operator's own sentences, never rewritten, only left out or reordered. A forecast Vy has superseded is left out («Forsinkelse forventes» once «Forsinket» is published), as is a sentence an earlier message already said (the shared cause), and advice («Ta neste tog ...») comes after the facts. Exact repeats only: two messages that differ in a place name are both kept. Built from the `has_situation` situations only, so null when there is none (a `KIX:` situation alone); absent from an event minted before the field existed.

situations_text_en.description: `situations_text` in English, from the same messages: null until every one of them has its English, rather than mix languages. It is a translation when any of those situations has `en_machine_translated` true -- present it as one.

situations_text_nn.description: `situations_text` in nynorsk, from the same messages: null until every one of them has its nynorsk, rather than mix bokmål into it. Every operator message's nynorsk is a machine translation (`nn_machine_translated` true), so present this as one. Absent from an event minted before the field existed.

summary.description: The journey definition's one-sentence summary, in Norwegian: the same sentence journey-alerts serves as its top-level `summary`, over every alert-worthy train on the definition at mint and not only this one -- for a favourites row («Signalfeil ved Asker: 4 tog er innstilt og 2 kan bli forsinket», «Tog L1 07:18 er innstilt, 2 til kan bli forsinket»). A snapshot at mint: a later change to the definition's trains mints nothing, so read journey-alerts for the current sentence. Null when there is nothing to say, which is never all-clear. Absent from an event minted before the field existed.

summary_en.description: `summary` in English, the same sentence in the same shape («Train L1 07:18 is cancelled, 2 more may be delayed»). The cause leads only when the operator published it in English too; otherwise this line names the trains without it, so the two can differ there and only there. Null exactly when `summary` is. Absent from an event minted before the field existed.

summary_nn.description: `summary` in nynorsk, the same sentence in the same shape («Tog L1 07:18 er innstilt, 2 til kan bli forseinka»). The cause leads only once the situation's `summary_nn` has been translated; otherwise this line names the trains without it, as `summary_en` does. Null exactly when `summary` is. Absent from an event minted before the field existed.

alternative_journey.description: The best remaining way there, which is not necessarily a faster one: for a cancelled train it legitimately arrives later than the timetable promised, so read `arrives_before_original` rather than assuming a saving.
